question_text: What is the difference between composition and aggregation in UML/OOP?
explanation: Composition: whole owns parts (same lifecycle). Aggregation: whole uses parts (independent lifecycle). In Java: composition = field initialised in constructor. Aggregation = passed as parameter. Oracle's ORM uses both.
solution: Composition: same lifecycle (part dies with whole). Aggregation: independent lifecycle (part survives whole's deletion).

question_text: What is the difference between abstract factory and factory method design patterns?
explanation: Factory Method: one product type. Abstract Factory: family of products (e.g., UI toolkit: createButton() + createCheckbox() + createScrollbar() — all for same OS theme). Oracle's SQL parsing uses Abstract Factory for different SQL dialects.
solution: Factory Method: one product, subclass decides. Abstract Factory: family of related products, ensures consistency across product family.

question_text: What is the difference between HTTP status codes 401, 403, and 404?

question_text: What is a REST API and what are the 6 REST constraints?
explanation: REST: Representational State Transfer (Fielding, 2000). 6 constraints define RESTful architecture. Statelessness is most critical — each request contains all needed info. HATEOAS: responses include links to next actions.
solution: REST 6 constraints: Client-Server, Stateless, Cacheable, Uniform Interface, Layered System, Code on Demand (optional).

REST constraints: (1) Client-Server separation, (2) Statelessness (no session state on server), (3) Cacheability (responses must indicate cacheable/non-cacheable), (4) Uniform Interface (resource identification, self-descriptive messages, HATEOAS), (5) Layered System (client unaware of intermediaries), (6) Code on Demand (optional — send executable code).

question_text: What is the difference between TCP's congestion control and flow control?
explanation: Flow control: receiver-to-sender feedback via rwnd in TCP header. Congestion control: sender-side cwnd adjusted by slow start, congestion avoidance, fast retransmit, fast recovery. Both limit send rate but different concerns.
solution: Flow control: protect receiver (rwnd). Congestion control: protect network (cwnd). Effective window = min(rwnd, cwnd).

options.option_text: Flow control applies to the entire network

Flow control: prevents sender from overwhelming the RECEIVER — receiver advertises window size (rwnd). Congestion control: prevents sender from overwhelming the NETWORK — sender maintains congestion window (cwnd). Effective send window = min(rwnd, cwnd). Flow control is end-to-end; congestion control is network-aware.
Congestion control uses the receiver window

question_text: What is the difference between mutex locking and spinlocking? When does Oracle Database use each?
explanation: Mutex: sleep-based, no CPU waste during wait, OS overhead for sleep/wake. Spinlock: CPU-intensive busy-wait, no OS overhead, only efficient if critical section is shorter than sleep/wake cost. Oracle: latches = spinlocks for short in-memory ops.
solution: Mutex: sleep (no CPU waste, OS overhead). Spinlock: busy-wait (CPU waste, no OS overhead). Use spinlock only for microsecond critical sections.

options.option_text: Mutex locking is only for user-space code

Mutex: thread sleeps while waiting (yields CPU, OS reschedules). Good for long wait times. Spinlock: thread busy-waits in a loop consuming CPU. Good for very short critical sections (microseconds) where sleep+wake overhead exceeds wait time. Oracle uses mutexes for long operations, spinlocks for short in-memory structures (latches).

question_text: What is an inode in Linux and what information does it store?

solution: Inode: metadata (permissions, owner, size, timestamps, block pointers). NOT file name. Directory entry maps name → inode number.

options.option_text: Inode: data structure storing file metadata — file type, permissions (rwx), owner UID/GID, timestamps (atime/mtime/ctime), file size, pointer to data blocks (direct, indirect, double/triple indirect). Does NOT store file name — names stored in directory entries pointing to inodes.
Each directory has one inode for all files
Inode stores the file name and contents

question_text: What is demand paging and what is the working set model?
explanation: Demand paging: lazy loading reduces startup time, wastes less RAM. Working set W(t,Δ): pages referenced in (t-Δ, t). OS tracks working set — if process's working set fits in RAM: it runs efficiently. Thrashing: working set > available frames.
solution: Demand paging: lazy page loading. Working set: actively used pages in time window. Keeping working set in RAM prevents thrashing.

options.option_text: Demand paging is slower than pre-paging in all cases
Working set includes all pages ever accessed
Demand paging loads all pages at process start

Demand paging: pages loaded into RAM only when accessed (page fault). Working set model: set of pages a process actively uses in a time window Δ. Keeping working set in RAM prevents thrashing. If sum of working sets > RAM: some processes must be swapped out.

question_text: What is the difference between hard links and symbolic (soft) links in Linux/Unix?
explanation: Hard link: inode reference. Soft link: path reference. Hard link survives original deletion (ref count). Soft link breaks when original deleted. Hard links cannot cross filesystem boundaries or link to directories (typically).
solution: Hard link: inode reference (survives deletion, same filesystem). Soft link: path reference (breaks if original deleted, crosses filesystems).

options.option_text: Hard links work across different filesystems

Hard link: directly references the inode — same file, multiple directory entries, inode reference count incremented. Deleting original doesn't affect hard link. Cannot cross filesystems. Symbolic link: references file path — if original deleted, symlink is broken. Can cross filesystems. Oracle uses hard links for database file management.
Symbolic links cannot be created in Linux

question_text: What is the difference between RANK(), DENSE_RANK() and ROW_NUMBER() in SQL window functions?
explanation: Example with scores 100,100,90,80: ROW_NUMBER=1,2,3,4. RANK=1,1,3,4. DENSE_RANK=1,1,2,3. Oracle uses all three in analytics — crucial for reporting.
solution: ROW_NUMBER: no ties. RANK: ties+gaps. DENSE_RANK: ties+no gaps. Key for Oracle reporting and analytics.

options.option_text: ROW_NUMBER(): unique sequential number, no ties (1,2,3,4). RANK(): same rank for ties, leaves gaps (1,1,3,4). DENSE_RANK(): same rank for ties, no gaps (1,1,2,3). Use ROW_NUMBER for pagination, RANK/DENSE_RANK for leaderboards.

question_text: Explain the difference between OLTP and OLAP. How does Oracle differentiate its products for each?

question_text: What is Oracle's MVCC (Multi-Version Concurrency Control) and how does it achieve read consistency?
explanation: Oracle MVCC: before-image stored in undo tablespace. Long-running queries reconstruct old version from undo if data was changed. SCN timestamp ensures read consistency. No dirty reads, non-repeatable reads prevented at SERIALIZABLE level.
solution: Oracle MVCC: undo segments store old versions. Readers see consistent snapshot at query SCN. Readers never block writers.

options.option_text: MVCC only works with SELECT statements
MVCC uses table locks for all reads
MVCC requires exclusive locks for reads

MVCC: Oracle maintains multiple versions of data rows using undo segments. Readers never block writers; writers never block readers. Each query sees a consistent snapshot as of its SCN (System Change Number). Dirty reads impossible — readers see committed state at query start time.

question_text: What is a B+ Tree index and why does Oracle Database use it as the default index structure?
explanation: B+ Tree advantages: internal nodes store more keys (higher fan-out = shorter tree). Leaf linked list enables efficient range scans. O(log n) guaranteed. Hash index is faster for equality but B+ Tree supports both equality and range.
